A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spectrum from Defocus work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures throughout. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix or the separately referenced supplement; supplement-only material cannot be compared.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulated reconstruction results in Table 1 and Figure 3, prototype measurements, ColorChecker evaluation, and robustness experiments in Figures 4–6.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulations, a low-exposure comparison, prototype reconstructions against measured spectral ground truth, and sensitivity experiments in Table 1 and Figures 3–5.

M1.justification: The two-lens architecture, forward model, spectral eigenspace projection, deep denoiser and fast plug-and-play ADMM reconstruction remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 has identical updates. Revised calibration bands and measurement counts configure the existing method rather than introduce a new algorithm.

E1.justification: Harvard, KAIST, CAVE and the same real-scene types are represented in both versions. However, v1's dataset declaration cites Brainard data, whereas v2 replaces that citation with Harvard, already evaluated in v1's Table 1. No identifiable Brainard-specific results establish whether this represents removed coverage or a citation correction.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from six to eight comparators by adding Spectral DefocusCam and 2in1 Cameras, both also evaluated in Figure 3. The existing comparators remain. These additions substantially broaden comparison with closely related defocus imaging and diffractive optical systems.

E3.justification: Simulated photon flux changes from 4.6×10^17 to 7.5×10^17 photons/m²/s, and v2 adds a 2.9-second exposure condition. Prototype calibration changes from 12 bands spanning 400–694 nm at 12 lens positions to 29 bands spanning 440–720 nm at five positions. V2 also evaluates real reconstructions against LCTF-measured spectral ground truth, extending v1's chart-reference and RGB evaluation.

E4.justification: V2 adds a targeted low-exposure robustness comparison and ground-truth failure insets in Figure 3. Depth and measurement-count sensitivity analyses remain in Figure 5, with revised curves; v1's explicit three-versus-six-measurement image comparison is not reproduced. The newly mentioned denoiser-versus-l1 ablation is only referenced to the unavailable supplement.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Additional averages and result entries in v2 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces SfD's PSNR/SSIM/SAM of 24.10/0.61/36.51 with 30.81/0.92/7.35, alongside extensive comparator-score revisions and new rows. These are not same-setting gains because photon flux changes. V2 adds per-channel real-scene scores and all 24 ColorChecker spectra, reporting average patch PSNR 29.54 dB and SAM 7.42°. Figure 3 and sensitivity curves also change.

T1.justification: The supplied forward model, optimization objectives, constraints and ADMM equations are unchanged, as are the principal optical assumptions. V1's explicit XYZ and color-difference calculations disappear, but these document standard evaluation computations rather than new theory. Neither PDF includes the referenced supplementary derivations.

C1.justification: The central claims of accurate, photon-efficient hyperspectral imaging using simple optics and subsecond reconstruction remain. V2 additionally claims that prototype performance matches simulation and explicitly highlights a preliminary comparative advantage under photon-starved conditions. These extend the performance claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands mechanism and limitation discussion. Long-wavelength errors are attributed to flattening chromatic focal shift rather than v1's lower illumination explanation. It adds low-rank spectral oversmoothing, dark-region light leakage and dynamic-range failures, possible remedies, and the need for more realistic low-light noise models. It also develops interpretations of comparator-specific artifacts.

D1.justification: V2 substantially revises acquisition documentation, specifying a tungsten–halogen source, 100 µm pinhole, LCTF sampling, spectral ground-truth capture, flat-target absorption correction, and an 800×800 crop from 1920×1200 images. Conversely, v1's exact lens model identifiers and approximately 25-lux scene illumination are absent from the supplied v2 text. Both retain a general code/data availability statement.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially across CASSI reconstruction, diffractive and metasurface imaging, and focal-stack predecessors. V2 explicitly distinguishes SfD from Spectral DefocusCam and 2in1 Cameras and discusses earlier spectral recovery by He et al. and Zhan et al. This clarifies its positioning around robust reconstruction and simple optics.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental discussion and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Experiments are reorganized into simulation settings, simulation results, data collection and real-data results, replacing the earlier system-specification and quantitative/qualitative subsection structure. Detailed colorimetry exposition is removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is relocated and its comparison chart changes axes and visual encoding. Figure 3 gains comparator columns, failure insets and a low-exposure panel. Figure 4 combines expanded real-scene and ColorChecker displays, replacing presentations previously spread across Figures 4 and 6. Figure 5 swaps panels and changes distance-axis coordinates; Table 1 expands structurally.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens real-world validation: v1 mainly shows RGB scene reconstructions and three ColorChecker spectra, while v2 supplies measured spectral ground truth, per-channel comparisons across four scenes, and all 24 patch spectra. Relevant new comparators and explicit failure analysis further improve scrutiny of the central claims. Some reproducibility details are lost, and changed settings prevent interpreting higher scores as direct gains, but the stronger spectral validation provides a substantial overall improvement.
